items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A skater who pushes a wall and rolls backwards opens the lesson.

Two spring balances show that **forces come in pairs**: Newton's **third law**. A book on a table separates **balanced forces** from **action–reaction pairs**, and two skaters show why the pair **does not cancel**.

The law then explains **walking**, **rockets** and **recoil**.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• contact and non-contact forces (friction, gravitational, magnetic)

• balanced forces and net force; Newton's first law

• Newton's second law, a = F ÷ m, and weight, W = mg

• friction opposes slipping of two surfaces in contact

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** State Newton's third law and identify action–reaction pairs.

**2.** Explain why action–reaction forces do not cancel.

**3.** Explain walking, rocket propulsion and recoil, and the role of friction in walking.

**What this shows**

• Left: a girl on roller skates pushes a wall.

• Right: a moment later she rolls **backwards**, away from the wall.

**Answer to Question 1**

**Backwards**, away from the wall.

**Answer to Question 2**

Take a few guesses. **Do not reveal the answer yet.** The wall pushed her; Practice 1 comes back to it.

**Answer to Question 3**

She would roll back **faster**.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Two spring balances hooked together. **Balance A** is fixed to the wall; a hand pulls **Balance B**, which reads 20 N. Balance A's reading is hidden.

**Answer to Question 4**

Also **20 N**.

**Answer to Question 5**

**Balance B** pulls A to the right; **Balance A** pulls B to the left.

**Answer to Question 6**

**30 N.** The two readings always match.

items.text:
**What this shows**

(a) A bat hits a ball. (b) The Earth and an apple. (c) Two magnets with like poles facing. Each arrow is labelled **on** which object and **from** which.

**Answer to Question 7**

The **ball pushes the bat backwards**. The batter feels this jerk in the hands.

**Answer to Question 8**

The **apple pulls the Earth up**, with an equal force.

**Answer to Question 9**

**Yes**, with equal and opposite forces. The pairs exist for **non-contact** forces too.

items.prompt: Complete the pair. A swimmer pushes the water backwards with her hands. Reaction:
options: the water pushes the swimmer forwards
the water pushes the swimmer backwards
the swimmer pushes the water forwards
her hands push her body forwards

items.prompt: True or false? When you kick a ball, the ball pushes back on your foot only after it starts moving.
options: True: the ball pushes back once it moves
False: both forces act at the same instant
True: the foot's force always comes first
False: the ball never pushes on the foot

items.prompt: A magnet pulls an iron nail towards itself with a force of 0.3 N. The force the nail exerts on the magnet is
options: 0.3 N, pulling the magnet towards the nail
0.3 N, pushing the magnet away from the nail
less than 0.3 N, towards the nail
zero, as the nail is not a magnet

items.text:
**On Question 1**

**A**: the water pushes the swimmer **forwards**.

**On Question 2**

**B**: **false**. Both forces act at the same instant, for as long as the foot and the ball are in contact.

**On Question 3**

**A**: **0.3 N**, pulling the magnet **towards the nail**.

items.text:
**What this shows**

A book at rest on a table, with the table's upward push on the book and the Earth's pull on the book (its weight).

**Answer to Question 10**

$F_{\text{on book from table}}$, the **table's upward push** of 10 N.

**Answer to Question 11**

**No.** Both act on the **same object**, the book, and they are different kinds of force. They are **balanced forces**.

**Answer to Question 12**

$F_{\text{on table from book}}$: the **book pushes the table down**.

script.x: Show the book. Pointer 1 sets it up.
Questions 10 to 12 in order. Answers are on pointers 2 to 4.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 13**

$F_{\text{on Earth from book}}$: the **book pulls the Earth up**.

**Answer to Question 14**

The first is **always** equal, by the third law. The second is equal only because the table is strong enough to hold the book.

script.x: Questions 13 and 14. Answers are on pointers 1 and 2.
Show the key idea.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Riya (40 kg) on skates pushes her friend Kabir (60 kg) with 120 N on a smooth floor. Kabir's push on her is hidden.

**Answer to Question 15**

**120 N**, in the opposite direction.

**Answer to Question 16**

**No.** One 120 N force acts on **Kabir** and the other acts on **Riya**. Each skater has a net force of 120 N.

**Answer to Question 17**

Riya: 120 ÷ 40 = **3 m/s², backwards**. Kabir: 120 ÷ 60 = **2 m/s², forwards**.

**Answer to Question 18**

**Riya.** The forces are equal, but she has **less mass**.

items.prompt: A book rests on a table. The reaction to the Earth's pull on the book is
options: the table pushing the book up
the book pushing the table down
the book pulling the Earth up
the Earth pulling the table down

items.prompt: Two children on skates, of masses 30 kg and 50 kg, push each other apart with a force of 150 N. Their accelerations are
options: 5 m/s² and 3 m/s², in opposite directions
3 m/s² and 5 m/s², in opposite directions
1.875 m/s² each, in opposite directions
5 m/s² and 3 m/s², in the same direction

items.prompt: A bar magnet and a compass needle attract each other with equal forces. The needle swings round but the magnet stays put, because
options: the magnet pulls harder than the needle does
the light needle gets a large acceleration; friction holds the heavy magnet
only the magnet exerts a force
the forces cancel on the magnet

items.text:
**On Question 1**

**C**: swap the names: the partner of $F_{\text{on book from Earth}}$ is $F_{\text{on Earth from book}}$. (A) balances the weight, but acts on the same object.

**On Question 2**

**A**: 150 ÷ 30 = **5 m/s²** and 150 ÷ 50 = **3 m/s²**, in opposite directions.

**On Question 3**

**B**: the needle is very light and free to turn, so the force gives it a **large acceleration**. The magnet is much heavier, and friction from the table holds it.

items.text:
**What this shows**

(a) A foot pushing off a **dry, rough floor** while walking, with the forces between the foot and the floor.

**Answer to Question 19**

**Backwards.**

**Answer to Question 20**

**Forwards.** This forward push from the ground is what moves us.

**Answer to Question 21**

**Friction.** It stops the foot from slipping backwards.

script.x: Ask Questions 19 to 21 first. The figure labels the answers, so keep it hidden.
Reveal (a) to check. Pointer 1 sets it up; answers are on pointers 2 to 4.

items.text:
**What this shows**

(b) The same step on a **wet, polished floor**: very little friction, and the foot slips backwards.

**Answer to Question 22**

There is **very little friction**, so the foot slips backwards and the floor cannot push us forwards.

**Answer to Question 23**

To **increase friction**, so that the ground can push us (or the vehicle) forwards without slipping.

script.x: Ask Questions 22 and 23, then reveal (b). Pointer 1 sets it up; answers are on pointers 2 and 3.
Show the key idea.

items.text:
**What this shows**

A rocket at lift-off: the engine pushes gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up, and the rocket's weight acts down.

**Answer to Question 24**

It pushes the rocket **upwards** with an **equal force**.

**Answer to Question 25**

When the upward push of the gas is **greater than its weight**, so the net force is upwards.

**Answer to Question 26**

**Yes.** It pushes on its **own exhaust gas**, not on the air.

**Answer to Question 27**

The gas pushes it **backwards**, so it **slows down**. The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 did this to land softly on the Moon.

script.x: Ask Question 24 first, then reveal the rocket. Pointer 1 sets it up.
Questions 25 to 27 in order. Answers are on pointers 2 to 5.

items.text:
**What this shows**

A cannon firing a ball: the cannon pushes the ball forwards, and the ball pushes the cannon backwards.

**Answer to Question 28**

The **ball**, with an equal force. This backward motion is called **recoil**.

**Answer to Question 29**

The cannon has a **much larger mass**, so its acceleration is much smaller. A gun recoils in the same way when it fires a bullet.

items.prompt: Fill in the blanks: When we walk, the foot pushes the ground ____, and the force of ____ from the ground pushes us ____.
options: forwards; friction; backwards
backwards; friction; forwards
backwards; gravity; forwards
forwards; weight; forwards

items.prompt: A rocket can speed up in empty space because
options: it pushes against the air
its exhaust gas pushes it
there is no gravity in space
its weight becomes zero

items.prompt: A gun of mass 3 kg fires a bullet of mass 30 g. The force on the bullet in the barrel is 600 N. The accelerations of the bullet and the gun are
options: 20 000 m/s²; 200 m/s², backwards
20 m/s²; 200 m/s², backwards
200 m/s² each, in opposite directions
20 000 m/s²; zero, as the gun is held

items.text:
**On Question 1**

**B**: backwards; **friction**; forwards.

**On Question 2**

**B**: there is no air in space to push against; the rocket pushes the gas, and the **gas pushes the rocket**.

**On Question 3**

**A**: force on the gun = 600 N, backwards (third law). Bullet: 600 ÷ 0.03 = **20 000 m/s²**; gun: 600 ÷ 3 = **200 m/s²**, backwards.
